title: Naked Soul
text:
I am a naked soul in these verses,

a naked soul that, anguished and alone,

leaves its petals scattered.


A soul that may be a poppy,

that may be a lily, a violet,

a crag, a forest, and a wave.


A soul that, like the wind, wanders restless

and roars when it is over the seas,

and sleeps sweetly in a cleft.


A soul that adores upon its altars

gods who do not stoop to blind it;

a soul that knows no barriers.


A soul that would be easy to master

with just a heart that broke open

to water it with its warm blood.


A soul that, when spring arrives,

tells lingering winter: return,

let your snow fall upon the meadow.


A soul that, when it snows, dissolves

in sadness, crying out for the roses

with which spring wraps us.


A soul that at times releases butterflies

into the open country, without setting a distance,

and tells them: sip from all things.


A soul that must die of a fragrance,

of a sigh, of a verse in which one begs,

without, if it can, losing its elegance.


A soul that knows nothing and denies everything

and, denying what is good, brings about the good

because it is by denying that it gives itself most.


A soul that often finds delight

in touching souls, despising the trace,

and feeling a caress in its hand.


A soul always discontented with itself,

wandering, running, turning like the winds;

a soul that bleeds and raves without cease

to be the star's ship underway.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated “Alma que” anaphora and the poem’s shifting natural forms, allowing the Spanish rhyme to give way to clear English images.

title: Facing the Sea
text:
Oh sea, enormous sea, fierce heart
of uneven rhythm, wicked heart,
I am softer than that poor stick
rotting, imprisoned in your waves.


Oh sea, give me your tremendous wrath,
I spent my life forgiving,
because I understood, sea, I gave myself away:
“Pity, pity for the one who most offends.”


Vulgarity, vulgarity hounds me.
Ah, the city and man have bought me.
Make me possess your nameless wrath:
this mission of a rose tires me now.


Do you see that vulgar man? He grieves me,
I lack air, and where it fails, I remain;
I wish I did not understand, but I cannot:
it is the vulgarity that poisons me.


I grew poorer because understanding overwhelms,
I grew poorer because understanding suffocates,
blessed be the strength of the rock!
I have a heart like foam.


Sea, I dreamed of being as you are,
there in the afternoons when my life
opened beneath the warm hours...
Ah, I dreamed of being as you are.


Look at me here, small, wretched,
every pain overcomes me, every dream;
sea, give me, give me the ineffable resolve
to become proud, unreachable.


Give me your salt, your iodine, your fierceness,
Sea air!... Oh storm, oh anger!
Unhappy me, I am a thistle,
and I die, sea, I succumb in my poverty.


And my soul is like the sea, it is that;
ah, the city rots and confounds it,
this petty life that provokes pain,
if only I could free myself from its weight!


Let my endeavor fly, let my hope fly...
My life should have been horrible,
it should have been an uncontainable artery,
and it is barely a scar that always aches.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sea’s direct address, the repeated “vulgarity,” and the contrast between oceanic force and the speaker’s diminished life.

title: The Devilish Point Descends from Heaven...
text:
I

LOVE


The devilish point descends from heaven

with which you wound and deceive mortal flesh.

It comes smeared with divine tricks,

and heaven and earth join its poison.


The blood of a man that wells in the wound

blossoms into forests: its swelling reeds

of golden shadow split the entrails

of the dark sky, and their ascent asks a question.


In their vain waiting for the answer

the reeds bend their lofty heads.

The sky sets its blue gauzes aflame.


Black winds, behind the glass

of the stars, move great masses

of dead worlds through their outskirts.


II

THE WORK OF LOVE


You see roses and lilies in the thornbush;

you play at being: in one hand you hold,

a little emerald, the ocean;

you speak without a tongue, entangle destiny.


You plant your head in the divine blue

and your feet, antipodes, in the distant

reverse side of the world; and you make yourself sovereign,

and release the sun from its path.


You look at the horizon and your gaze

makes dawn be born in night;

you dream and your fictions create bone.


The hand that raised you in flight falls silent,

and at your feet the sky falls, broken glass,

and dust and shadow lift their heels.


III

LANDSCAPE OF DEAD LOVE


You are sinking now, sun; my waters are colored

with flames about to die; now my unraveled

heart falls, and night brings

edges that weep in the wind.


Already black herds are glimpsed

on opaque shores; already my tongue draws

the pitch of death; and the thorn

no longer turns aside from me; shadows devour me.


Dead hide, the sun lies down at last

like a dog turning upon its tail,

the earth lies down to rest, exhausted.


A bony hand extinguishes the stars:

their stony paths screech

with the black, fleshless pupil.
editorial_note: The three-part sequence and its typographic labels are preserved; “endiablada punta” is rendered as “devilish point” to retain the poem’s infernal, bodily force.

title: Oh, You!
text:
Oh you, who subdue me. Why have you arrived late?
Why have you come now, when the soul does not burn,
when I have no roses with which to make you
a joyful garland sprinkled with stars?


Oh you, whose word is sweet as the murmur
of fountain water; sweet as the cooing
of the turtledove; sweet as sleeping kisses
upon two pale hands that protect nests.


Oh you, who with your hands can take my head
and make flowers spring from it like a tree in festival
and make a smile arch between my lips
like a cloudy sky that suddenly iridesces.


Why have you arrived late? Why have you come now
when I have been vanquished by a destroying flame,
when I have been swept away by divine fire
and go, blinded and sad, along a black road?


I want, God of gods, to be made wholly new.
Let them weave me with lilies; let the hands of mystery
prune me; let them strip away my weeds.
Your lips were not made to cure sorrow.


For your lips, water of supreme purity.
For your lips, crystal cups and the pure-white foam
of a soul that knows nothing of bees,
nor of honeys, nor of crimson flowers.


For your hands, those that have never shrouded;
for your eyes, those that have never wept;
for your dreams, dreams like golden swans;
so that your pupils might pursue my traces,


Oh, if my petals then, crushed by your hands,
were to acquire superhuman powers by magic
and, made light, cling to the light of the stars
so that your pupils might pursue my traces.


Welcome the death you would give me by drinking me in;
welcome your fire that withers springs;
welcome your fire that kills the rosebushes:
let every corolla draw near your evils.


Oh you, whom I idolize above existence,
oh you, for whom I desire my essence renewed.
Why have you come now, when I will not achieve
the divine torment of seeing myself unpetaled?...
editorial_note: The translation preserves the apostrophe’s repeated “Oh you,” its floral imagery, and the final paradox of renewal through being stripped of petals.

title: Much Further Beyond
text:
And what if we keep moving ahead

from smile to smile

until the last hope?


So what?

And what do you give me,

me, who have lost my name,

the name that was sweet substance to me

in remote times, when I was not myself

but a girl deceived by her blood?


Why, why

this undoing of myself, this bleeding out,

this plucking myself, this losing my balance

if my reality retreats

as if driven back by machine-gun fire

and suddenly breaks into a run,

though they catch up with it all the same,

until it falls at my feet like a dead bird?

I would like to speak of life.

For this is life,

this howl, this driving one's nails

into one's chest, this tearing out

one's hair by handfuls, this spitting

into one's own eyes, only to say,

only to see whether one can say:

“Am I, then? Is it true that I am?

Is it not true that I exist

and am not the nightmare of a beast?”


And with muddy hands

we pound on love's doors.

And with conscience covered

in dirty and beautiful veils,

we plead for God.

And with temples cracking

with idiotic pride

we take life by the waist

and give death a sidelong kick.


For this is what we do.

We get ahead from smile to smile

until the last hope.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Pizarnik’s abrupt repetitions, bodily violence, and question marks as the poem’s central rhythm.

title: The Awakening
text:
Lord

The cage has become a bird

and flown away

and my heart is mad

because it howls at death

and smiles behind the wind

at my delusions


What will I do with fear

What will I do with fear


Light no longer dances in my smile

nor do the seasons burn doves in my thoughts

My hands have stripped themselves naked

and gone where death

teaches the dead to live


Lord

The air punishes my being

Behind the air are monsters

who drink my blood


It is the disaster

It is the hour of the not-empty emptiness

It is the instant to bolt the lips

to hear the condemned scream

to contemplate each of my names

hanged in nothingness.


Lord

I am twenty years old

My eyes too are twenty years old

and yet they say nothing


Lord

I have consummated my life in an instant

The last innocence exploded

Now it is never or nevermore

or it simply was


How do I not commit suicide before a mirror

and disappear to reappear in the sea

where a great ship would await me

with its lights on?


How do I not extract my veins

and make of them a ladder

to flee to the other side of night?


The beginning has given birth to the end

Everything will continue the same

The worn smiles

The interested interest

The questions from stone to stone

The gestures that mimic love

Everything will continue the same


But my arms insist on embracing the world

because they have not yet been taught

that it is already too late


Lord

Cast away the coffins of my blood


I remember my childhood

when I was an old woman

The flowers died in my hands

because the wild dance of joy

destroyed their hearts


I remember the black mornings of sun

when I was a child

that is, yesterday

that is, centuries ago


Lord

The cage has become a bird

and has devoured my hopes


Lord

The cage has become a bird

What will I do with fear
editorial_note: The translation retains the poem’s repeated invocations and paradoxes, including “the not-empty emptiness” and the cage that becomes and devours as a bird.

title: Paths of the Mirror
text:
I

And above all, look with innocence. As if nothing were happening, which is true.


II

But I want to look at you until your face draws away from my fear like a bird from the sharp edge of night.


III

Like a girl drawn in pink chalk on a very old wall, suddenly erased by the rain.


IV

As when a flower opens and reveals the heart it does not have.


V

All the gestures of my body and my voice to make of myself the offering, the bouquet the wind abandons on the threshold.


VI

Cover the memory of your face with the mask of what you will be and frighten the girl you were.


VII

The night of the two of us dispersed with the fog. It is the season of cold foods.


VIII

And thirst, my memory is of thirst, I below, at the bottom, in the well, I drank, I remember.


IX

To fall like a wounded animal in the place that was to be one of revelations.


X

As though it were nothing. Nothing at all. Mouth sewn shut. Eyelids sewn shut. I forgot.

Inside, the wind. Everything closed and the wind inside.


XI

To the black sun of silence the words turned golden.


XII

But silence is certain. That is why I write. I am alone and I write. No, I am not alone.

There is someone here, trembling.


XIII

Even if I say sun and moon and star I mean things that happen to me. And what did I desire?

I desired a perfect silence.

That is why I speak.


XIV

Night has the shape of a wolf's cry.


XV

Delight of losing oneself in the image intuited. I rose from my corpse, I went in search of who I am.

Pilgrim of myself, I have gone toward the one who sleeps in a country of wind.


XVI

My endless fall into my endless fall where no one awaited me, for when I looked to see who awaited me I saw nothing but myself.


XVII

Something was falling in the silence. My last word was I, but I meant the luminous dawn.


XVIII

Yellow flowers constellate a circle of blue earth. The water trembles, full of wind.


XIX

Dazzlement of day, yellow birds in the morning. One hand unties darkness, one hand drags

the hair of a drowned woman who never stops passing through the mirror. I must return to the memory of the body,

I must return to my grieving bones, I must understand what my voice says.
editorial_note: The numbered prose-poem sequence is preserved; source display wraps within sections are joined where needed so the English keeps each complete fragment together.

title: An Absence
text:
Oh! how sadly my soul complains!

If beautiful morning

with its rosy veil,

with placid harmony

greets me as it rises into high heaven,

I pine for my beloved

and my sigh greets the dawn.


If peaceful afternoon

with its banded, tranquil sky

smiling crowns me,

and if it cradles my brow

with delightful and perfumed air,

I grieve as well, because my soul

finds no peaceful calm without her.


If serene night,

full of peace and enchantment,

caresses me kindly,

if radiant light is shed

by the stars that rise high,

my sad eyes ask for light in vain,

her eyes do not illumine me!


How fortunate are those who, in absence,

find fate merciful

and see their beloved woman everywhere;

while to my sorrowful complaint

mute and eternal solitude replies!

Her pure image, her tender memory

are only remembrance, vain illusion...

Delightful morning,

enchanting afternoon, cold night,

oh! how sadly my soul complains!
editorial_note: The source’s “raDiosa” is treated as the obvious “radiant”; the translation keeps the poem’s repeated morning, afternoon, and night refrain.

title: A Wandering Bird
text:
Where do you direct your flight,

sad bird?

Perhaps, alas, you have lost

the token of your love?

Or perhaps the beautiful tree

where you kept your nest,

the ax has destroyed

or the scorching fire?


Your song, which one day there

sounded so pleasing,

will carry its plaintive note today

into the forest;

for it is only the memory

of happiness now lost

that will vainly ask an echo

of a beloved voice.


Like you, I too cross

the air in my flight,

like you I too long

and do not know what I am;

the tree of my cherished glories

has also died,

fleeing gloomy memories

I go like you.


My eyes also weep,

and my anxious word

is lost in sorrow

as it crosses the clouds,

my mind loses itself

in the darkness of fate,

like you, I without a path

give myself to wandering chance.


Ah! our night, O bird,

is sad and solitary,

how vague the prayer

of our solitude!

And what will become of both of us

on our wandering journey,

when the black storm

raises its voice?
editorial_note: The translation preserves the regular stanzaic movement and the poem’s deliberately unresolved question about the bird and speaker’s fate.

title: God Made the World; With His Divine Voice...
text:
God made the world; with his divine voice

he drew it from chaos,

and, admiring his wondrous work,

they say he loved it.


His grand desire had been fulfilled,

magnificent, immortal;

but still, as a lover, he had yet to pour out

his heavenly affection.


And before the sweet gaze of his tenderness

the sphere fell into ecstasy,

and the angel of light and beauty

was changed into the moon.


And the pleasing fragrance of his noble breath

he cast over April,

and the angel of perfume in that instant

became the rose of the garden.


And from his gracious lips he breathed

the angel of honey;

the sweet, faithful bee became an emblem

of its delicate nectar.


And from his voice he formed sympathy,

a seductive echo,

and the angel of placid harmony

was changed into a nightingale.


Yet powerful God desired

to form a new being;

and he mercifully brought an angel from his Eden

and you were that woman.


And he adorned you with a diadem of beauty,

raised you like a deity;

gave your eyes a thousand pearls of tenderness,

of joy and pity.


And as an emblem, O Celia, of divine love,

the Maker wished to consecrate you

to the beneficent destiny

of the angel of love.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem’s chain of metamorphoses from divine voice to moon, rose, bee, nightingale, and beloved woman.

text:

editorial_note: This text duplicates the preceding source poem apart from a minor accent difference; its translation is kept identical while retaining the supplied title.

title: To Mount Eden
text:
Why, as I climb the hill

that fiercely separates me from you,

O pleasant dwelling, my eyes

fill with sad tears?

Could it be, alas, that I will not return

to you, beloved dwelling?

Who knows, for death

accompanies man everywhere,

and perhaps it will make of this tender farewell

an eternal farewell;

or perhaps the heavens will wish,

sweet dwelling of my childhood,

that there, when fierce time

turns my head gray,

I may come to seek in your bosom

a solitary tomb.

Then you, beloved home,

with your ceibas and palms

will give peaceful shade

to my funerary resting place.

Or perhaps the hard hand

of wretched misfortune

will make you pass from my people

into strange hands, alas,

and when I return as a pilgrim

from my wearisome journey,

I will not find in you the faces

that once, in another age, delighted me;

perhaps the impious hurricane

or time that loves ruins

will turn you into mournful ruins,

without mercy for my soul.

Ah! then may heaven grant,

if it brings me back to your bosom,

that your new possessor

or the fury of the hurricane

respect the exile's

memories of childhood.
editorial_note: The translation retains the island-specific ceiba and palm imagery and the final appeal to an exile’s childhood memories.

title: Gloss
text:
Reason that reigns in me,

why must I lie,

saying impassively no,

when the soul says yes?


On looking at your beautiful eyes

I feel joy being born,

because they turn, my life,

anger into enchantment.

On looking at your red lips

where love is treasured

my enslaved breast adores you,

and, fleeing frenzy,

I must exclaim, my lady,

“reason that reigns in me.”


If you observe in my countenance

the delirium you inspire,

if you look at me with delight

and in my throbbing breast

perceive the sweet instant

you cause in my soul,

what is it worth that I feign calm!

if the fire that consumed me

triumphantly wins the palm,

why should I lie?


Oh! do not expect

the ardent breast to deny it;

so sweet an affection

cannot be hidden; to silence it

is to suffer and increase it:

for in vain, O God, would I lie

if, when asked someday

whether my heart adored you,

I answered, my soul,

saying impassively, NO.


It would be as good as denying

that you are beautiful and alluring,

that dawn appears evasive

if it sees your eyes shine;

it would be as good as claiming

that one who came to behold you

managed to live and forget you,

could manage to live without you,

if I said NO to loving you

when the soul says YES.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated yes/no refrain and the source’s glosa-like stanza progression; rhyme is allowed to yield to clarity in English.

title: To Goyita
text:
Goyita of my soul,

far from you,

pain torments

my loving breast.

Ah! who could

receive in your arms

fierce death!

For to me

it would be sweeter

than my life

when absent from you.

It is bliss

to live and not see you,

sweet beauty!

Seeking here a gift

to consecrate to you,

I find nothing of my own

to give you;

for in my meadow

everything dies, Goyita,

if you are away.

There is a single plant

green and flourishing,

thanks to my watering it

evening and morning;

I cultivate it

because it is a memory of you,

a living portrait.

It bears a fruit sweeter

than bees’ bread,

and in sweetness it resembles

your laments of love;

your pleasant breath

is echoed by its perfume

that scents the wind—.

Goyita, there is only one

that I send you,

born in my orchards

in summer.

The sun gilds it,

for of all fruits it is

queen and lady.

Its green and gold

is not as beautiful

as that of your lip,

precious crimson;

and in the countryside

there is no tastier fruit,

for it is… the pineapple.

Do you remember that day,

loving Goya,

when your beautiful mouth

gave me pineapple;

and without offending you

I took the pineapple

that was on your lip?

I do not know whether the one now

my love sends you

will be as sweet

as that of that day.

Ah! if only I could

take it from your lips

even if I died!
editorial_note: The closing pineapple image is kept as both literal fruit and remembered kiss; “pan de abejas” is rendered as “bees’ bread” rather than replaced with a more specific honey term.

title: To the Illustrious Bucolic Poet Bernardo de Balbuena
text:
ROSANIO

Where lies that shepherd, dear Belisa,

who to the sounds of a rustic shepherd's pipe

sang, in a tone that stunned the breeze,

your grace and beauty?

That one who, tender and simple, celebrated

the peasant peace, whose sweetness

left the woods and meadows

filled with gentle music?

“Balbuena” was his name,

and with one voice the shepherdesses and shepherds

whom he ardently loved

crowned his brow with laurel and flowers.

Answer me, Belisa; you who were

his kind confidante

and my beloved lavished

blameless affection upon you…


BELISA

Ah! he no longer exists!

his body sleeps in the tranquil tomb

of a Catholic temple,

serving Borinquen as a lofty example.

His silent grave

I would see with greater joy

if it were humbly offered in the fields.

Then, at the beloved cold stone,

as the day went down,

we would give fragrant

diadems of amaranths and roses.

His wheedling flutes

that gladdened valleys and riverbanks,

lie hanging from a leafy mamey tree,

and to the lamenting zephyr,

the soft wandering echoes

ask for the tune that once charmed them.


THE BARD

I heard your voices, my shepherds,

my tears fell like rivers

from my eyes,

but they yielded to the voice of truth.

Shepherds, no more weeping

if we mourn only his presence;

his essence still lives in us,

the echo of his golden flutes still sounds.

Over mountains and plains

his songs are recalled by

the wind in the banana trees,

the wind in the palm groves,

the light turtledove,

the lark's delightful song.

Within you, Rosanio, he left that pure

and tender love of the peasant

from the age that inspires envy,

when eternal struggle followed peace;

and in your eyes, Belisa, so affectionate,

two of his verses,

tender love's cooings,

sweetest and soft and ardent.

Borinquen inspired him; it deems itself heir

to his strains and to his noble

and gracious thoughts.

If beloved Balbuena,

born in Castile,

has his name treasured in its annals;

his golden age

was fulfilled in Puerto Rican peace;

and when he lost life's sweet radiance,

his loving soul, full of gratitude,

left his shepherd's pipe to these forests

and his generous tomb to Borinquen.
editorial_note: The dramatic exchange, named speakers, Borinquen, mamey tree, and pastoral bird imagery are preserved; “calandria” is rendered as “lark.”
